Definition: A high-level, mandatory document signed by senior management stating the organization's security intent and goals -- the "why" and "what," with no technical specifics.
A mandatory document defining the specific, measurable technical requirements (algorithms, thresholds, configurations) that make a policy enforceable.
The one optional document type in the hierarchy -- recommended best practices for meeting a standard, with no penalty for using another compliant method.
A mandatory, exact step-by-step set of instructions for a task; rewritten most often because it is tied to specific tools and versions.
A responsibility-assignment table mapping who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for a task, so ownership is unambiguous before an incident occurs.
A control principle that splits a high-risk action (such as approving a wire transfer) so that no single person can both request and approve it.
The "tone at the top" -- the degree to which senior executives actively fund and enforce the security program, proven through budget allocation and consistent enforcement.
The psychological manipulation of people into performing actions or revealing confidential information, trading on traits like helpfulness, deference to authority, and urgency.
A social-engineering attack using fraudulent communications (usually email) to trick a victim into revealing credentials, clicking a malicious link, or running malware.
A phishing attack tailored to a specific individual or department using prior research to make the message personally convincing.
A form of spear phishing aimed at high-profile executives (CEO, CFO) to authorize wire transfers or unlock the most sensitive assets.
Voice phishing -- social engineering conducted over the phone, often with spoofed caller ID or a cloned voice impersonating IT or a known employee.
SMS (text message) phishing that often exploits urgency, such as a fake CEO gift-card request.
Operational Security -- the practice of protecting small, individually harmless pieces of public information that an attacker could combine into something dangerous.
The ability to identify, process, and comprehend critical elements of one's environment to keep sensitive data from being exposed to an adversary.
Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies -- an executive IT-governance framework that defines the control objectives IT must meet (the "what").
Information Technology Infrastructure Library -- an IT service-management framework specifying day-to-day operational processes like ticketing and change management (the "how").
The management of data's availability, usability, integrity, and security across the enterprise, including its life cycle from creation to secure destruction.
The process of locating and producing digital evidence for civil or criminal proceedings; a legal hold overrides normal retention and deletion schedules.
Replacing sensitive fields in a copy of production data (names, card numbers) with realistic fake values so it is safe to use in staging while keeping the same structure.
Artificially generated data that statistically mirrors production data without containing any real user information.

An assessment is a less formal evaluation to find control gaps; an audit is a formal, evidence-based review against a standard, run internally or by an external third party; a certification is an accredited body's attestation issued after a successful external audit.

General Data Protection Regulation -- the EU privacy law giving individuals rights such as erasure and requiring informed consent where consent is the legal basis and 72-hour breach notification, backed by fines up to 4% of global revenue.
California Consumer Privacy Act (expanded by the CPRA) -- a California privacy law giving consumers the right to know, delete, and correct their data and to opt out of its sale or sharing.
Brazil's General Data Protection Law (Lei Geral) -- a privacy law closely modeled on GDPR.
Children's Online Privacy Protection Act -- a US law requiring verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13.

Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act -- a US law mandating safeguards and access logs for electronic Protected Health Information (ePHI); encryption is an addressable safeguard, and properly encrypted ePHI is exempt from breach notification.

Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard -- a contractual (not legal) standard from the card brands requiring controls such as unreadable stored card data; network segmentation is not mandatory but shrinks the cardholder data environment in scope.
Digital Markets Act -- an EU market-regulation law imposing interoperability, user-choice, and data-combination limits on designated "gatekeeper" platforms, with fines up to 10% of global turnover.
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 -- a voluntary framework organized around six functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) used as a common language for program maturity.
The international standard series for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS); ISO/IEC 27001 is the certifiable standard, and certification is granted after an external audit.
An auditor-attested report on a service provider's controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria; Type 1 covers design at a point in time, Type 2 covers operating effectiveness over a period.

Center for Internet Security products: Benchmarks are consensus hardening baselines for specific technologies, and the Critical Security Controls are a prioritized set of safeguards grouped into Implementation Groups.
The Cloud Security Alliance's Cloud Controls Matrix -- a cloud-specific control framework mapped to other standards.
The legal principle that digital data is subject to the laws and regulations of the country in which it is physically stored.
